summary:
Bahrain repealed its British colonial-era sodomy statute in 1976 and is the only Gulf state that does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy. No statute criminalises transgender expression as such. The 1976 penal code sets the age of adulthood for consensual same-sex acts at 21.

That baseline does not translate into safety from arrest. Police apply the morality and indecency provisions of the penal code, Articles 324, 329 and 350, which carry between three months and two years' imprisonment, fines of up to 200 Bahraini dinars, and deportation for non-Bahrainis. The government has used these articles against people suspected of being LGBTQI+ or of cross-dressing. In 2009 a man was sentenced to one month in jail for wearing an abaya and carrying a purse in public; in 2011 police raided a party described as a same-sex wedding. The Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation in February 2024.

Entry screening is a documented risk. The Interior Minister has stated that "suspected" effeminate homosexuals are barred from entering Bahrain and that airport checks are used to identify them. Bills before parliament have proposed expressly banning LGBTQ foreigners from entering the kingdom or holding residency permits. In September 2013 the Gulf Cooperation Council states agreed to discuss a proposal for testing to bar gay foreigners from entry; officials later retreated from it.

Legal gender recognition runs through the courts and is effectively closed. Judges require medical documentation of a "sex change operation" or of medical necessity before a marker can be changed. A 2023 ruling held that sex-reassignment procedures contravene Islamic law where the case is treated as arising solely from gender dysphoria, which confines eligibility in practice to people with intersex traits. In a May 2023 judgment a lower court refused a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and for gender-affirming care on Sharia grounds, and also refused the Ministry of Health medical-committee examination he had requested. Gender-affirming care is correspondingly restricted for anyone who needs it while in the country.

No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. Article 309 of the penal code protects religious groups from hate speech but extends no equivalent protection to LGBTQ people, and hostile speech against them carries no legal consequence.

Article 330 requires anyone charged with prostitution or "fujoor" to be taken to a hospital for sexually transmitted disease testing and allows relocation to a medical facility. For a trans person taken into custody, that provision places a compulsory medical examination inside the arrest process.

There is no LGBTQ community infrastructure to fall back on. The US Department of State records no approved LGBTQ-related organisations, and ILGA judges it improbable that any sexual- or gender-diversity group could register, since the body that approves associations may refuse any group judged contrary to morality or public order. No LGBTQ-specific shelters or facilities are documented.
tangentialFactors:
The legal position is contested in the source record. A Canadian Immigration and Refugee Board response of August 2016, covering 2011 to July 2016, reports that "according to sources, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain", citing a Canadian government report of 14 July 2016 and a Gulf News article of 5 February 2011. That conflicts with the 1976 decriminalisation reading carried by Wikipedia, Outright International and 2023 US State Department reporting, and the conflict is unresolved.

Independent scrutiny of Bahrain's record is thin. The authorities have for a decade denied entry to or obstructed UN human rights bodies and Amnesty International researchers, leaving local media as the only source for much of what happens inside the country.

Accusations of homosexuality are used as a political weapon. False allegations have been deployed to discredit government critics and protesters, including the human rights advocate Nabeel Rajab and participants in the 2011 Pearl Square demonstrations.

Hostility in the press is open. On 3 August 2024 the newspaper Albilad published a widely viewed caricature showing a roll of toilet paper printed with a pride flag, captioned "the correct place".
localsOnly:
Schools are a policy target. In October 2021 a bill was proposed that would have criminalised promoting or inviting others to homosexual gatherings, with up to five years' imprisonment. Other pending bills would instruct teachers to watch for signs of homosexuality or cross-dressing in children so that the children can be punished.

The Education Ministry disclaims responsibility for the subject. Assistant Under-Secretary Khalid Al Alawi told parliament that sexuality is a matter for parents, that "the public shouldn't make a big deal out of this problem because it does not exist", and that students whose appearance conflicts with school values should be disciplined.

Enforcement reaches school administrations. On 14 February 2024 the Ministry of Education referred a private school's administration and its entire board for investigation and dismissed the school's general manager after a video circulated showing two male students pretending to propose to each other in class. A 2022 incident in which a private school distributed material perceived as promoting homosexuality prompted calls for stricter legislation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 1976 decriminalisation date rests on ILGA-sourced and Wikipedia infobox material and on Outright International's country page; no Bahraini statute text confirming the repeal was located in this inventory. The Canadian Immigration and Refugee Board's 2016 finding that homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain is not reconciled with that reading.

The September 2013 Gulf Cooperation Council proposal to test and bar gay foreign nationals was discussed but never adopted; officials publicly retreated from it, and no implementing measure is documented.

The bills restricting entry and residency for LGBTQ foreigners, the October 2021 gatherings bill and the proposed teacher-guidance measures are recorded as proposals. Whether any has been enacted is not established by the sources here.

Violence data specific to trans people in Bahrain is not sourced in this inventory.
